predictions.selection_reason: defines regex pattern -> used to detect trailing semicolons -> affects cookie parsing logic
predictions.source_summary: The regex is used in parse() function to detect trailing semicolons in cookie strings. Cookie strings come from external sources (Set-Cookie headers).
predictions.sink_summary: The parse() function processes cookie strings to create Cookie objects. If strict mode is false, trailing semicolons are removed; if strict mode is true, cookie strings with trailing semicolons are rejected (return undefined).
predictions.guard_summary: In strict mode, trailing semicolons cause parse() to reject the cookie string entirely (line 308). In non-strict mode, trailing semicolons are trimmed before further parsing. Additional validation includes regex matching for cookie pairs and attribute validation.
predictions.risk_pattern: Trailing semicolon handling creates a discrepancy between strict and non-strict parsing modes. In non-strict mode, trailing semicolons are silently removed, potentially allowing malformed cookies that would be rejected in strict mode. This could lead to parsing inconsistencies when the same cookie library is used with different strictness settings.
used_variable_sources: str parameter of parse() function (cookie string from Set-Cookie header)
predictions.context_summary: TRAILING_SEMICOLON regex is used in the parse() function to check for trailing semicolons in cookie strings. According to RFC 6265 S4.1.1, trailing semicolons are not part of the specification. In strict mode, cookies with trailing semicolons are rejected; in non-strict mode, they are trimmed before parsing.
unresolved_facts: Whether any downstream code depends on the strict/non-strict behavior difference
Whether malformed cookies with trailing semicolons could bypass validation in non-strict mode
Whether this discrepancy could be exploited in mixed strictness environments
